However, such trajectories are scarce in long-horizon software engineering tasks, where a minor error can invalidate the entire rollout. Repeatedly restarting from the initial state is commonly used yet inefficient, and resetting only the context with working directory misses state changes such as installed dependencies. Therefore, branching from intermediate steps to preserve earlier progress requires restoring both the agent context and execution environments. In this paper, we present SPROUT ( S na P shot-based R oll OUT ), an agentic RL rollout framework that scales long-horizon coding tasks by resuming and branching from intermediate states. Specifically, SPROUT was built on top of a lightweight infrastructure that checkpoints both the filesystem and the agent context after each assistant turn. A verifier-guided backtracking policy then selects where to resume a failed attempt and how to proceed. Extensive experiments on long-horizon coding tasks show that SPROUT achieves up to 23.6% improvement over pass@k across various LLMs, while using 32 32 – 52 % 52\% of their tokens. For RL training of Qwen3.8-27B, SPROUT stably outperforms standard GRPO by 13.9 13.9 points on three long-horizon coding benchmarks while cutting the time per training step by 39.5 % 39.5\% . SPROUT thus makes RL on long-horizon coding tasks both more effective and cheaper to scale. For such tasks, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the de facto training paradigm ( Shao et al., 2024a ; He et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026 ) : the agent attempts a task in an executable environment, a verifier such as the task’s test suite checks the final result, and the policy is updated from these outcomes. Such training is especially expensive on long-horizon tasks. A single attempt may read a large, unfamiliar codebase, install dependencies, build artifacts, and run test suites, and it can take hours to finish. The longer the task, the harder it is to learn from. The verifier reward is usually binary, so an attempt receives credit only if its final solution passes. Over a long attempt, one wrong decision anywhere, such as an incorrect patch after hours of correct setup, is enough to make the reward zero, and successful attempts become rare as the horizon grows. In group-relative methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024a ) , a task whose attempts all fail has zero advantage for every attempt and contributes no gradient. The expensive rollouts spent on the hardest tasks thus produce no learning signal, even when most of their steps were correct. Two strategies are commonly used to obtain more positive signal. The first samples more attempts per task ( Brown et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2022 ) , which multiplies an already high cost: every new attempt redoes its exploration and setup from scratch and can repeat the same mistake. The second branches from intermediate steps of earlier attempts. In a coding environment, this requires three things. The restored environment must match the agent’s context at the branch point, including the files the agent edited, the packages it installed, and the artifacts it built anywhere in the system. Checkpoints must be cheap enough to take at every step, since any step may turn out to be the right place to branch. The branch point itself must also be chosen well. Existing methods miss at least one of these requirements. Tree search and reflection methods ( Yao et al., 2023a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ) , as well as CBPO ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , branch only within the conversation. Among RL methods that restore sandbox states, Shepherd ( Yu et al., 2026 ) versions only the agent’s workspace, BPO ( He et al., 2026a ) snapshots containers only at a few selected steps, and both rely on layered container snapshots with hard limits on depth. Full virtual machine snapshots are complete but must store guest memory at every step, making the storage requirement unacceptable on long horizon tasks. To choose branch points, BPO uses policy entropy without consulting the verifier, and Shepherd delegates the choice to a stronger external model. Their RL experiments focused on tasks normally take 8 - 25 steps, leaving long horizon unexplored. Figure 1: SPROUT: branch from checkpoints instead of restarting. Resuming a failed rollout from the step where it went wrong beats resampling it from scratch, at inference time and in RL. (a) DeepSWE, four models: SPROUT beats Pass@4 on every model while spending 48–68% fewer tokens; Shepherd and entropy-based branching do not. (b) Guided by verifier feedback, the same agent policy resumes from paired context and VM checkpoints to explore new continuations. In this paper, we present SPROUT ( S na P shot-based R oll OUT ), an agentic RL rollout framework that scales long-horizon coding tasks by resuming and branching from intermediate states. Sprout is composed of three components: 1) a restorable execution layer runs each attempt in a microVM ( Agache et al., 2020 ) and take a snapshot of its filesystem incrementally after every assistant turn, pairing each checkpoint with the matching agent context. 2) a verifier-guided backtracking policy decides where to branch (Figure 3 ): the actor itself reviews failed trajectories with the verifier’s feedback, chooses where to resume, and proposes the first action of the new continuation, so the recovered trajectories do not import knowledge from a stronger model. 3) a GRPO-based training procedure learns from the branched rollouts and distills the guidance used during search into the base policy. We evaluate SPROUT on various mainstream long-horizon agentic coding benchmarks, i.e., DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard. Compared with a single attempt per task, SPROUT raises the resolve rate on DeepSWE from 72.3 % 72.3\% to 98.2 % 98.2\% with Kimi K3, from 46.9 % 46.9\% to 82.3 % 82.3\% with Claude Sonnet 5, and from 42.5 % 42.5\% to 85.8 % 85.8\% with GPT 5.6 Luna, exceeding four independent attempts while using 32 32 – 52 % 52\% of their tokens. For RL, we train Qwen3.8-27B with SPROUT on a subset of SWE-bench Rebench v2. Relative to the base model, training raises the resolve rate from 62.7 % 62.7\% to 84.3 % 84.3\% on SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard, from 37.2 % 37.2\% to 40.7 % 40.7\% on DeepSWE, and from 49.4 % 49.4\% to 64.0 % 64.0\% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, ahead of standard GRPO on the same tasks ( 74.5 % 74.5\% , 33.6 % 33.6\% , and 39.3 % 39.3\% ) while cutting the 39.5% of the time per training step. 2 Related Work Long-Horizon Coding Agents. Coding agents solve software engineering tasks by interleaving reasoning with tool calls in interactive environments ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Dong et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Frameworks such as Mini-SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024b ) , OpenHands ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , OpenCollab ( Hsu et al., 2026 ) , and Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025 ) let them navigate repositories, edit code, and validate changes through execution, and benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified ( OpenAI, 2024 ) , SWE-bench Pro ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , DeepSWE ( Huang et al., 2026b ) , and Terminal-Bench 2.1 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) evaluate them on increasingly long-horizon tasks. A single attempt can span tens to hundreds of tool calls and fail on a single error, after which it is usually discarded and resampled from scratch, redoing progress such as understanding the repository and localizing the root cause. SPROUT instead resumes failed attempts from intermediate states and reuses their prior progress. Tree Search and Backtracking. Repeated sampling increases task coverage but restarts every sample from the initial state ( Brown et al., 2024a ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Tree-search methods instead expand and backtrack over intermediate states ( Yao et al., 2023b ; Hao et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) , much as Go-Explore first returns to a visited state and then explores ( Ecoffet et al., 2021 ) , while reflection methods correct errors in later attempts using verbal or tool feedback ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Gou et al., 2024 ) . In software engineering, SWE-Search ( Antoniades et al., 2025 ) applies Monte Carlo tree search to issue resolution, and Shepherd ( Yu et al., 2026 ) delegates the choice of where to intervene over reversible traces to a stronger external model. Because agents edit files, install packages, and build artifacts, branching only within the conversation, as tree search and reflection methods do, leaves the environment inconsistent with the agent’s context, and Shepherd versions only the agent’s workspace. SPROUT restores the full filesystem together with the matching agent context and lets the actor itself, rather than a stronger model, use verifier feedback to choose where to branch and how to continue. In sparse-reward agent tasks, groups whose attempts all fail are common and yield no gradient under group-relative methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024b ) . Several RL methods therefore branch from intermediate states, including VinePPO ( Kazemnejad et al., 2024 ) for advantage estimation, TreeRL ( Hou et al., 2025 ) for process supervision, SPARK ( Wu et al., 2026 ) at critical states identified by the agent’s own decision signals, CBPO ( Wang et al., 2026b ) for contrastive branching, and BPO ( He et al., 2026b ) with container snapshots. However, most of these methods branch only within the conversation, which in coding environments leaves the environment inconsistent with the agent’s context, while BPO can resume only from a few steps selected by policy entropy without consulting the verifier, so neither approach supports consistent branching from an arbitrary tool boundary. Among checkpointing mechanisms ( Wang and Zheng, 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , layered container snapshots ( Merkel and others, 2014 ) have hard limits on depth and full microVM snapshots ( Agache et al., 2020 ) must store guest memory at every step. SPROUT checkpoints the full filesystem incrementally after every tool call and pairs each checkpoint with the matching agent context, so any tool boundary can be restored with low storage overhead and without re-executing the prefix, enabling more efficient exploration to obtain learning signals. 3 SPROUT SPROUT is a rollout framework for long-horizon agentic tasks, it allows resuming execution from any recorded intermediate state of an earlier attempt and explore alternative continuations from that state. We first formulate the rollout collection problem and give an overview of the framework. We then describe the execution layer that enables resumption and the verifier-guided backtracking policy that determines where to resume and how to continue. Local access requires the environment and the agent context to describe the same point of an attempt. Boundary t t of τ i \tau_{i} is eligible , t ∈ ℰ ⁡ ( τ i ) t\in\mathcal{E}(\tau_{i}) , if a filesystem checkpoint was taken after all tool calls of turn t t completed and the conversation prefix can be recovered up to and including the observation o t o_{t} . Search branches only from eligible boundaries, so every continuation starts from the observations and execution state of its selected prefix. Any guidance for a new continuation is stored separately from that prefix. Filesystem restoration under the harness contract. Each attempt runs in its own microVM ( Agache et al., 2020 ) , so a checkpoint covers the whole guest filesystem, including dependencies and build artifacts outside the working directory. Our harness executes every tool call as a synchronous shell command and disallows background processes, so by the end of a turn no process started by the agent is still running, and all state that persists across turns lives on disk. Restore \operatorname{Restore} therefore boots a fresh microVM from the saved filesystem and reinitializes the tool runtime, and guest memory never needs to be captured. Together with the recovered context, this gives the continuation the full state of its prefix under the stated harness constraints. Incremental checkpoints and isolated branches. After each turn, the execution layer records the changes to the VM disk as an incremental block-level OverlayBD layer. Consecutive checkpoints share all unchanged content, so the storage a checkpoint adds grows with the blocks written during the turn rather than with the size of the environment. Each restored branch writes to its own copy-on-write layer over the saved history, so several continuations can inherit the same progress without affecting one another or their parent. Incremental storage and isolated writes together make it practical to checkpoint every turn of a long trajectory. 3.4 Verifier-guided Backtracking Policy Restoration makes earlier states available; the search policy decides which of them are worth continuing from. We instantiate it with verifier-guided backtracking, in which the actor π θ \pi_{\theta} also analyzes failures and plans branches under separate role prompts. The roles share parameters, and only the analysis and planning roles see feedback from completed attempts, so no separate analyst or reviewer model is involved. From failure evidence to branch decisions. For each newly failed attempt τ i \tau_{i} , the policy writes an analysis z i z_{i} of why the attempt failed, which of its progress can be reused, and which eligible boundaries could plausibly lead to a successful continuation. Because the procedure uses diagnostic feedback beyond the binary reward, these experiments measure exploration in a setting where such feedback is available, not unassisted agent performance. 3.5 Policy Optimization with Branched Rollouts Training reuses the same restoration and repair mechanisms to construct groups. During search, the reviewer sees diagnostics that never appear in the actor’s ordinary context. Training aims to transfer the resulting corrective behavior into the actor while accounting for the prefixes that trajectories in a group share. Constructing training groups. Each task receives a fixed-size group: two independent roots and K = 3 K=3 retained children per root, for eight evaluated attempts. This specializes the collection framework to a single layer of children. If at least one root succeeds (TT or TF), the reviewer selects one usable boundary per root, and that root’s children continue from it without an injected starting turn. If both roots fail (FF), the reviewer uses verifier feedback to rank boundaries and attaches a corrective direction to each. A starting turn is then written from each visible prefix and its direction, filtered by a judge, and executed in the restored environment before the actor continues. A boundary is usable only if it is eligible and its prefix leaves room for the continuation within the context budget. Algorithm 1 (Appendix B ) specifies the oversampling, independent-rollout fallbacks, and task replacement that keep every group at eight attempts. Learning without the review context. For a guided branch, the learner sees the retained prefix, the starting turn, and the executed continuation, but not the diagnostic analysis or the corrective direction. The policy is therefore trained to produce corrective turns from the context it has during ordinary execution. Removing the review context from the learner’s input does not remove its influence on how the sample was generated. Overall, SPROUT achieves high task coverage while substantially reducing execution and inference costs. On DeepSWE, SPROUT matches or exceeds Pass@4 across all four models, using 53.5–69.1% fewer execution steps and 47.9–67.7% fewer tokens. The improvement is particularly clear with GPT 5.6 Luna: the resolve rate increases from 68.1% to 85.8%, while token usage decreases from 1,409M to 652M. With Kimi K3, SPROUT reaches a 98.2% resolve rate using only 32.3% of the tokens required by Pass@4. It also improves over Shepherd by 9.7–23.0 percentage points across the four models while consistently using fewer steps and tokens. Recovery rates of 64.8–93.6% further show that failure- guided backtracking can resolve a substantial fraction of initially unsuccessful tasks. SPROUT also compares favorably with alternative adaptive sampling strategies. With Qwen3.8-27B, it achieves a 78.6% resolve rate and a 64.8% recovery rate, compared with 71.7% and 54.9% for entropy-based sampling, while reducing token usage from 8,589M to 4,123M. Its largest improvement over Pass@4 is obtained with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Table 3 ), where the resolve rate increases from 66.3% to 89.9%. This gain of 23.6 percentage points is achieved with 38.6% fewer execution steps and 61.3% fewer tokens, together with an 80.0% recovery rate. As a result, SPROUT maintains competitive task coverage at much lower cost, demonstrating that SPROUT effectively uses failure feedback to identify recovery points and achieve a strong balance between task resolution and sampling cost. The token-efficiency advantage of depth comes with sequential dependencies: each review round requires trajectories and verifier feedback from the preceding round. Branches within a single round can, in principle, execute concurrently, potentially reducing per-task latency. Intermediate configurations such as 2 × 4 2\times 4 and 4 × 2 4\times 2 therefore trade off feedback depth against intra-task parallelism. Our current implementation executes branches within each round sequentially, so the reported results characterize the success–token trade-off and do not measure the latency achievable with parallel branching. 5 Conclusion In this paper, we have proposed SPROUT ( S na P shot-based R oll OUT ), a framework that addresses the scarcity of verified positive trajectories in long-horizon agent learning by resuming failed rollouts from any intermediate snapshot. Combining copy-on-write filesystem checkpointing, step-aligned conversation restoration, and verifier-guided backtracking, it lets agents backtrack to an earlier state and reuse the trajectory up to that point rather than re-executing it from scratch. Across multiple models and coding benchmarks, SPROUT matches or exceeds repeated independent sampling at a fraction of the token cost, and in RL training it improves the base policy on all benchmarks while outperforming GRPO with shorter training steps. By transforming failed rollouts into cost-effective starting points for exploration, SPROUT provides a practical foundation for collecting positive supervisory signals and scaling autonomous agent capabilities. We use the 113-task public DeepSWE, the 89-task Terminal-Bench 2.1, and the 51-task SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard. Sampling experiments use Kimi K3, Qwen3.8-27B, Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and GPT 5.6 Luna with fixed model weights. Kimi K3 runs with reasoning effort set to max , and all other models run with reasoning effort set to high . In SPROUT , the actor also performs failure analysis and branch selection under separate role prompts, with the same reasoning effort as its actor role. Execution environment. All runs use mini-swe-agent ( Yang et al., 2024a ) with a sandbox shell as the environment interface. Shell calls are synchronous, and background processes are disabled. SPROUT checkpoints the full filesystem after each turn and pairs it with the corresponding agent context. Each branch resumes in an isolated sandbox. DeepSWE attempts run offline with 2 CPUs, 8 GB of memory, and a time limit of 10,800 seconds. Baselines. Independent sampling performs four fresh attempts per task. Appendix C Starting Turns versus User Hints A guided branch needs some way to carry the corrective direction into the restored context. We considered two formats. User hints. The simplest format is a user hint : an external message, appended to the restored context, that states the corrective direction. Because the hint is derived from verifier feedback, it tends to leak into the continuation. The actor often recites the message, quotes test names or expected values from it, or justifies later actions by referring to it, so the continuation depends on information that is unavailable during ordinary execution. The hint also causes a problem for training. It is not an action of the policy and must be removed from the learner’s context. Once it is removed, the training context no longer explains the continuation: turns that recite or respond to the hint remain in the trajectory without a visible cause. Starting turns. SPROUT instead writes the guidance as a starting turn a j ′ a^{\prime}_{j} in the actor’s own voice, consisting of brief reasoning followed by tool calls whose observations come from real execution (Section 3.4 ). The turn must read as a natural continuation of the prefix and may not mention checkpoints, other branches, or hidden tests, and in training groups a judge filters turns that violate these constraints (Appendix B ). The context therefore contains no foreign message. During training, a j ′ a^{\prime}_{j} remains in place as an ordinary policy turn, and only the review context used to write it is removed (Section 3.5 ). The actor thus learns the corrective action itself rather than how to respond to an external hint. Appendix D State Projection and Cache Matching Efficiency Motivation. In agentic reinforcement learning for long-horizon coding tasks, rollouts frequently traverse identical or semantically equivalent intermediate states (e.g., repository navigation, virtual environment configuration, dependency installation). Re-executing these initial setup steps from scratch wastes compute budget, while naively snapshotting and restoring complete microVM environments can introduce severe I/O contention. To amortize rollout overhead, SPROUT incorporates a state-matching mechanism that identifies whether an intermediate execution state can be directly resumed from an existing checkpoint. This appendix provides a detailed empirical comparison of our state projection approach against representative caching and hashing baselines. Experimental Protocol and Baselines. We evaluate caching mechanisms on 248 rollout trajectories (136 generated with GPT 5.6 Luna and 112 with Qwen as query policies) collected across the 134 candidate tasks that initially failed single-pass exploration. We evaluate five configurations: • No Cache : The standard baseline that disables state reuse entirely, executing every trajectory prefix from scratch. • Exact Full History : Matches intermediate execution states strictly by verifying identical raw conversational histories and tool-call logs. • Official TVCACHE TCG : The official Tool Call Graph (TCG) prefix-matching implementation from TVCACHE ( Kumar et al., 2026 ) , a stateful execution cache designed for agent post-training. • Full-Workspace Hash (Upper Bound) : Computes recursive SHA-256 cryptographic hashes across the entire microVM workspace filesystem after each tool step to detect identical on-disk states. This represents the empirical upper bound of state-level hit rates. • Ours (Scan-free Relaxed Projection) : Projects filesystem mutations into lightweight metadata signatures at tool boundaries without recursive disk-tree traversal, filtering out superficial non-deterministic side effects.
